title: Your Smart Home Can't Reliably Tell Your Pets Apart
hook: Two gadget reviews, same failure: an AI litter box that swapped one cat's identity for another's, and a Google camera feature that forgot which pet was which.
key_points: The Verge's reviewer found Whisker's AI litter robot attributed visits to the wrong cat.
Google's Pet Memory for Gemini for Home, meant to name pets in camera alerts, lost track of hers.
Both features promise recognition of a specific individual — the hardest version of the task.
Recognition is a probability, not a lookup: similar-looking pets, odd angles, and dim light all degrade it.
The health and safety pitches ('flag illness early', 'only alert me for what matters') depend on that shaky identification.
content_html: Two of The Verge's recent smart-home reviews landed on the same complaint from opposite directions. Whisker's AI-powered litter robot, which is supposed to log which cat used the box, credited visits to the wrong animal — as reviewer Jennifer Pattison Tuohy put it, the machine thought her cats had swapped bodies. Google's new Pet Memory feature for Gemini for Home, meant to name individual pets in camera notifications, forgot who her cats were.
extra_html:
Both products are attempting the hard version of a vision task. Detecting "a cat" is close to solved; deciding which cat, from a ceiling camera, in changing light, when the two animals look alike, is a probability estimate that quietly gets it wrong. That's not a bug the way a crashed app is a bug — it's the normal behavior of a classifier operating near its limits.

It matters because the marketing rests on the identification. "Spot health changes in your cat's litter habits" and "only notify me about the dog" are only as good as knowing who's who. A useful habit with any AI feature that claims to recognize a specific individual — pet, person, or product — is to check its work before trusting the conclusions built on top of it.

related.title: What AI Can't Do
related.hook: Today's AI can write a sonnet and flunk a question a child gets right. Knowing its hard edges — no real understanding, no live truth, no common sense — is what makes you good at using it.

related.title: AI in Everyday Tools
related.hook: You've used AI for years without calling it that — every time your phone unlocks with your face, your maps reroute around traffic, or your inbox filters spam.

related.title: When AI Makes Things Up
related.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

flashcards.prompt: Why do consumer AI features struggle to identify a specific pet?

choices.text: Recognition is a probabilistic guess that degrades with similar animals, angles, and lighting
The cameras don't record video at all
Pets move too fast for any camera to capture

flashcards.explanation_html: Telling one individual from another is far harder than spotting "a cat." Two similar animals, an unusual angle, or poor light can flip the guess.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a mistaken pet ID matter beyond being annoying?
flashcards.back_html: The selling point is health and filtering — "this cat's litter habits changed", "only alert me for the dog." Wrong identity makes those insights worthless.
